newsitem.title: THAILAND: Sahaviriya Steel hopes rusty business will shine.
newsitem.headline: Sahaviriya Steel hopes rusty business will shine.

text.p: Loss-making Sahaviraya Steel Industries of Thailand expects business to improve now that anti-dumping duties are being imposed on cheap steel imports from Russia, Ukraine and Poland.
"This (imposition of anti-dumping duties) will benefit not only Sahaviriya but also the industry as the whole," SSI's managing director Adisak Lowjun told Reuters.

Preliminary anti-dumping duties of about 25 percent to 52 percent on structural steel and hot-rolled sheets from the three countries were imposed by Thailand's from late December after complaints from the hard-hit domestic steel industry.

Before the duties were set, lower quality imported steel from the three countries was sold at about $250 per tonne, well below prices in the sellers' domestic markets, and far les than SSI's price of about $340 per tonne.
"But whether the company will be able to make profits or not will depend on a lot of factors. If the market and the economy improves, we hope to be able to operate profitably," he said.
With the imposition of the tariff and improving market conditions, the firm planned to raise output to 70 percent of plant capacity from about 54 percent in 1996, Adisak added.
Production at its southern Prachuab Khirikan plant would increase to 1.7 million tonnes, he said.

SSI was granted investment incentives by the government in 1989 to build Thailand's first mills for making hot-rolled, cold-rolled and electro-galvanised steel. Its products are used in a range of applications, from steel pipes to furniture.
The company started producing hot-rolled steel in February 1994. Its capacity is approximately 2.2 million tonnes.

But tough market conditions coupled with cheaper imports hit the company hard. In 1995, the company reported net losses of 189 million baht ($7.56 million) which grew to 1.64 billion baht at the end of the first nine months in 1996.
SSI's share price has plunged to 8.70 baht from 50 baht when it was first offered to the public.

Adisak estimated that Thai demand for steel this year would reach 2.5 million tonnes from 2.4 million in 1996. The company plans to export up to 20 percent of its products and sell the rest domestically.
But he added the export target could be reduced if domestic demand rose.
He said the company hopes to be able to raise prices, adding that a desirable spread between steel slab, the raw material and finished product prices should be about $150 per tonne.
SSI is currently operating at a spread of about $90 per tonne, with a hot-rolled coil price of $340 per tonne and a slab price of $250 per tonne.
"But again, it depends on market condition. If there is no demand, who will buy expensive products? Any price adjustment will be based on market conditions and not the anti-dumping tariff," he said.
However, analyts doubted the company would be able to turn huge losses into profit this year even though its overall performance would likely improve.

"The long-term outlook is good. We expect the company's performance to improve. But the immediate outlook is not rosy, the company has a big, expensive inventory that they need to use up," said Thanawat Patchimkul, analyst at Seamico Securities.

"Nevertheless, we believe the company is reaching its critical point," he said, adding that SSI's inventory, which the industry estimated at around 250,000 tonnes, would be used up by the first half of 1997.
(US$1 = 25 baht)
